All seven components identified in the dust continuum are associated with corresponding \[C II\] emission, confirming that the dust continuum detected within LAB1 is also at $z\approx3.10$.
The 860 $\mu$m maps uncover an extended structure of dust emission on a 60 kpc scale, which is decomposed to eight individual components (ALMA1–ALMA7, and the Bridge).
ALMA5 is blank in the rest-frame UV and optical images, in contrast with its bright \[C II\] emission.
A remarkable example is ALMA5, which has no counterpart at near-infrared or optical wavelengths, while a rotating disk structure is suggested by its \[C II\] emission.
About 80$\%$ of the molecular gas is concentrated in ALMA1+2+5.
We found that the majority of this gas mass is concentrated near the Ly $\alpha$ peak.

Spatially resolved \[C II\] and infrared luminosity ratios for the widely distributed media ($L_{\rm [CII]}/L_{\rm IR}\approx10^{-2}-10^{-3}$) suggest that the observed extended interstellar media are likely to have originated from star-formation activity and the contribution from shocked gas is probably not dominant.
As shown in Figure 6, the $L_{\rm [CII]}/L_{\rm IR}$ ratios in LAB1 are broadly consistent with those observed in local galaxies.

Considering the data, therefore one possible scenario is that we are witnessing a merging phase of multiple galaxies hosted in multiple halos. If they are merging and not yet virialized, the velocity offsets are expected to be small as observed in LAB1.
LAB1 seems to be multiple-merging phase involving a number of galaxies and halos on a group scale, which may be a progenitor of a Bright Cluster Galaxy.

While (primarily obscured) star-formation activity in the LAB1 core is one of the most plausible power sources for the Ly $\alpha$ emission, multiple major-mergers found in the core may also play a role in making LAB1 exceptionally bright and extended in Ly $\alpha$ as a result of cooling radiation induced by gravitational interactions.

all_quotes.loc: The central heating source and scattering scenario
all_quotes.quote: Considering the Ly $\alpha$ luminosity of LAB1, L$_{\rm Ly\alpha}\approx10^{44}$ erg s$^{-1}$, therefore the star-forming activities can power the Ly $\alpha$ emission if the escape fractions are high enough ($f_{\rm esc, Ly\alpha}\gtrsim20\%$).

However, it is not clear whether or not star formation in the galaxies in solely responsible. We suggest that cooling radiation induced by strong gravitational interactions may also play a significant role.

Massive star-forming galaxies are easily enshrouded by dust in an intensely star-forming phase, and often undetectable in the optical to NIR (e.g., (cite: 2020A&A...640L...8U) and references therein). Furthermore, the molecular/fine-structure lines at these wavelengths provide powerful tools to characterize the nature and conditions of the interstellar medium (ISMs) in galaxies.

To extract spatially extended emission and also perform an angular-resolution-matched comparison with CO(4–3) and 860 $\mu$m data, we also produce $1.0^{\prime\prime}$ and $1.4^{\prime\prime}$ cubes in the same way but applying varying $uv$-tapering and 80 km s$^{-1}$ velocity bins.
The C40–1 array configuration utilized was the most compact configuration at the time (baseline lengths of 15 to 279 m), which was suitable to detect extended components.
To isolate the emission from each component, bright sources were sequentially modeled and subtracted using casa/imfit.
This process allows us to effectively extract extended emission from the data cube, suppressing the influence of noise.
Since it is not straightforward to isolate line fluxes from the cube in this crowded region, we derive line properties for groups on the basis of 1.4$^{\prime\prime}$ resolution data.

We note that there is currently no evidence to support AGN activity in LAB1 ((cite: 2009ApJ...700....1G)), although we cannot exclude the possibility that there is a heavily obscured AGN present. Nevertheless, the observed range of $L_{\rm [CII]}/L_{\rm IR}$ is higher than the value reported for $z=1-2$ AGNs (log($L_{\rm [CII]}/L_{\rm IR}$)$\sim-3.5$ for AGNs with $10^{13}-10^{14}L_{\rm IR}$, (cite: 2010ApJ...724..957S)), which is also consistent with a lack of AGN activity.
In LAB1, the galaxies are distributed within a region expected if they are bounded in a halo with $\lesssim10^{12}$ $M_\odot$. However, this scenario is highly unlikely.
Hence the stellar-mass-halo mass relation, which is derived from clustering analysis, suggests a halo with $\sim10^{13}$ $M_\odot$ (e.g., (cite: 2015A&A...576L...7D)).

all_quotes.quote: We cannot detect any \[C II\] (and dust continuum emission) from K1 and so our observations also do not support the idea that K1 is a member of LAB1. We do not include this source in discussion in this paper.

$\dagger$ Some fraction of fluxes of fainter sources may be underestimated due to difficulty of source deblending. $\ddagger$ Upper limits are shown only for the brightest three sources since the beam size is too large to isolate limits on fainter sources.

We note that it remains unclear whether or not all of the emission observed by the single-dish telescope is completely recovered by ALMA or not, as the remaining uncertainty ($0.7\pm1.2$ mJy) indicates.
These estimates, however, are based on single point photometry and thus remain uncertain.

Although, the current estimate has relied on SED templates of bright dusty star-forming galaxies due to the shortage of photometry; this may overestimate the dust temperature for an intergalactic region (or a region in the outskirts of a galaxy) and thus underestimate the $L_{\rm [CII]}/L_{\rm IR}$.

We note that a caveat is the influence of line of sight projection on the measured velocity dispersion. While a simple, spherical geometry is assumed in deriving the track of escape velocity in Figure 7, this may not the case.
